The selection algorithm

Likely organism → susceptibility → site exposure → PK/PD strategy → patient risks → narrowest workable regimen. A drug can cover the organism on paper and still fail because it cannot reach the compartment or is inactivated there.

Check local antibiogram for empiric choices; use isolate susceptibility when available. Factor in renal/hepatic function, age, body size, pregnancy, critical illness/burns, GI absorption, allergy phenotype, interactions, cost and dosing convenience (slide 5 and transcript).

Normal-to-drug bridge

Normal bacterial processDrug intervention
Build a cross-linked wallPBPs: beta-lactams; D-Ala-D-Ala substrate: vancomycin; early MurA step: fosfomycin
Maintain membrane integrityDaptomycin (Gram-positive); polymyxins (Gram-negative)
Translate proteins using 30S + 50S30S: aminoglycosides/tetracyclines. 50S: macrolides/clindamycin/linezolid. Fidaxomicin is the RNA-polymerase exception.
Make nucleic acids and folateDNA: fluoroquinolones/metronidazole by different mechanisms. Sequential folate blockade: TMP–SMX.

Cidal kills; static inhibits growth and relies on host clearance. The lecture does not establish universal clinical superiority of cidal drugs. Site, organism, exposure and host immunity matter (slide 9).

Additional agents mentioned in the slides
Additional slide examplesLecture distinction
Cefoxitin / cefuroximeSecond generation: cefoxitin adds anaerobic coverage; cefuroxime does not. Slide 13.
Ceftazidime ± avibactam; ceftaroline / ceftobiproleCeftazidime: Pseudomonas; avibactam broadens selected resistance coverage. Ceftaroline/ceftobiprole: MRSA-active cephalosporins. Slide 13.
CefiderocolReserved resistant Gram-negative option; susceptibility and specialist input matter. Slide 13.
Imipenem–cilastatin; newer inhibitor combinationsImipenem is not interchangeable with meropenem susceptibility. Vaborbactam/relebactam extend selected KPC coverage; aztreonam–avibactam addresses selected MBL-producing organisms. Slide 14.
Minocycline, tigecycline, eravacycline, omadacyclineMinocycline: selected Stenotrophomonas/Acinetobacter, IV:PO 1:1. Tigecycline: broad resistant-organism role but substantial nausea. Eravacycline/omadacycline: expensive reserved roles; omadacycline IV:PO is not 1:1. Doxycycline is the lecturer’s priority. Slide 28.
Amantadine / rimantadineInfluenza uncoating/M2 blockers shown historically; high resistance means not routine current influenza therapy. Slides 48,55.

Compare two options

Name what they share, then identify the difference that changes the answer.

Master comparison

Drug/familyCoverage & siteMost useful discriminator
Penicillin VK / GStreptococci; penicillin G also syphilis. IV G for serious streptococcal disease/neurosyphilis; IM benzathine G for appropriate syphilis stages.Formulations are not interchangeable. Depot benzathine is not the neurosyphilis formulation.
Nafcillin / oxacillin / dicloxacillinMSSA and susceptible staphylococci; nafcillin/oxacillin IV for serious infection, dicloxacillin PO for mastitis/SSTI.MSSA coverage does not imply MRSA coverage.
Amoxicillin–clavulanateStreptococci, susceptible Gram-negatives, additional anaerobic coverage; pneumonia, SSTI, bite wounds. Not Pseudomonas.The inhibitor restores activity against certain enzymes; it does not make the combination cover every resistant organism.
Ampicillin–sulbactamSusceptible Gram-negatives, streptococci and anaerobes. Not Pseudomonas.Do not extend this combination-specific CNS warning to ampicillin alone; ampicillin has established CNS uses.
Piperacillin–tazobactamGram-negatives including susceptible Pseudomonas, streptococci, anaerobes; severe polymicrobial/hospital infections.Unlike cefepime, already supplies anaerobic coverage. Do not routinely add metronidazole for duplicate coverage.
Cefazolin / cephalexinMSSA and streptococci; cefazolin IV for surgical prophylaxis/serious MSSA; cephalexin PO for susceptible skin and urinary infections.A penicillin allergy label alone does not automatically exclude cefazolin; severe delayed reactions need specialist assessment.
CeftriaxoneEnhanced Gram-negative coverage; meningitis, SBP, UTI, gonorrhea; useful typical bacterial pneumonia coverage.Not antipseudomonal; not MRSA therapy. Broad Gram-negative does not mean every Gram-negative.
CefepimeBroad Gram-negative coverage including susceptible Pseudomonas; serious hospital infections.No reliable anaerobic coverage. Lecture says no ESBL coverage: do not choose it as the dependable ESBL solution.
Ceftolozane–tazobactamResistant Gram-negatives, including susceptible Pseudomonas and some ESBL-producing organisms.An inhibitor does not overcome every resistance mechanism; generation numbering is less useful than the specific spectrum.
ErtapenemESBL-producing Enterobacterales and anaerobes; some Gram-positives.No Pseudomonas or Acinetobacter. The major carbapenem exception in this lecture.
MeropenemESBL-producing Enterobacterales, susceptible Pseudomonas, anaerobes; possible Acinetobacter depending on susceptibility.Broad spectrum is not a reason to use it unnecessarily. No routine need for additional metronidazole.
AztreonamAerobic Gram-negatives including susceptible Pseudomonas; no Gram-positive or anaerobic coverage.Not a complete regimen for mixed Gram-positive/anaerobic infection.
VancomycinIV: Gram-positive organisms, including MRSA. PO: C. difficile in gut lumen. Resistance especially in E. faecium.Route is part of the answer. Oral vancomycin does not treat MRSA bacteremia. Infusion flushing is not automatically an IgE allergy.
Dalbavancin / oritavancinGram-positive infections; approved SSTI uses. Lecture describes off-label osteomyelitis/endocarditis regimens.Long half-life improves convenience but prolonged exposure matters if an adverse reaction occurs; severe-infection schedules are not interchangeable with single-dose SSTI treatment.
DaptomycinMRSA and VRE; bloodstream and skin infection contexts.Pulmonary surfactant inactivates it: do not use for pneumonia. Poor CNS penetration also limits use.
Polymyxin B / colistinMDR Gram-negatives, including susceptible Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter; substantial intrinsic gaps.Lecture shorthand “colistin = prodrug” refers to IV colistimethate, not the active colistin molecule. Usually reserved alternatives; inhaled use is adjunctive.
Azithromycin / clarithromycin / erythromycinAtypical respiratory coverage; azithromycin used in CAP regimens, traveler diarrhea and selected mycobacteria. Clarithromycin in selected H. pylori/mycobacterial regimens; erythromycin often used for GI motility.Pneumococcal macrolide resistance matters. H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis are not “atypical” organisms despite the transcript grouping.
FidaxomicinC. difficile treatment in the gut lumen.Slide 25 says fosfomycin in this location; transcript corrects the intended drug to fidaxomicin. It is not systemic therapy.
Doxycycline / tetracycline familyDoxycycline: atypical CAP, tick-borne disease, Chlamydia. Tetracycline: H. pylori.Doxycycline does not prolong QT: useful distinction from macrolides. Lecture prefers better-studied alternatives when Legionella is strongly suspected; short pediatric courses can have specific indications.
LinezolidMRSA, VRE, pneumonia/SSTI; toxin suppression. Static against staphylococci/enterococci, cidal against most streptococci.One SSRI is not the same risk context as multiple serotonergic exposures; assess interactions rather than declaring universal safety. Unlike daptomycin, useful in pneumonia.
ClindamycinGram-positives/anaerobes if susceptible; adjunct toxin suppression in necrotizing infections; selected prophylaxis/topical uses.It reduces new toxin synthesis; it does not directly bind and neutralize preformed toxin. Resistance limits routine empiric use. Slide 2–20% refers to diarrhea, not a proven C. difficile rate.
GentamicinEnterobacterales; synergy with cell-wall agents in selected severe Gram-positive infections. Lecture: not a clinical Pseudomonas option.Do not choose it for Pseudomonas based on older class summaries. Synergy regimens have their own dosing, not automatic high-dose extension.
TobramycinPseudomonas—lecture calls it the best aminoglycoside choice—and Enterobacterales.Usually combined with a non-aminoglycoside outside uncomplicated UTI; class membership does not make gentamicin equivalent.
AmikacinEnterobacterales, susceptible Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter; selected Nocardia/NTM/TB combination regimens.An inhaled indication is formulation-specific; do not assume all aminoglycosides have the same spectrum or route.
MetronidazoleAnaerobes, selected protozoa; adjunct IV therapy in fulminant C. difficile, not routine replacement for oral luminal treatment.Cefepime may need added anaerobic coverage; pip-tazo/meropenem/ertapenem already provide it.
TMP–SMXSusceptible Gram-positive/negative organisms, MRSA, Stenotrophomonas, PJP treatment/prophylaxis; UTI/SSTI. Lecture cautions against relying on it for streptococci.Do not use total tablet milligrams for TMP-based dosing. Toxicities generally become more relevant at higher doses/longer courses.
NitrofurantoinLower urinary infection, especially susceptible E. coli; bactericidal in urine.Good bladder levels do not mean good blood or renal-parenchymal levels. Fever/flank pain makes uncomplicated cystitis logic fail.
Fosfomycin (oral)Main lecture role: susceptible E. coli cystitis; Enterococcus including selected VRE. Do not assume Klebsiella/Pseudomonas outcomes are reliable.Not fidaxomicin, not a macrolide, not the oral answer to every MDR infection.
Ciprofloxacin / levofloxacin / moxifloxacinTranscript identifies ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin as oral antipseudomonal options when susceptible.Do not extend ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin Pseudomonas coverage to moxifloxacin. This guide does not invent a missing follow-up lecture.
OseltamivirInfluenza A/B treatment; selected prophylaxis. Start early; treat hospitalized/severe/high-risk patients even beyond 48 h.Release, not entry, uncoating or protease processing. Do not combine multiple neuraminidase inhibitors.
Zanamivir / peramivirInfluenza A/B. Route differentiates them.Slide says all require renal adjustment; inhaled zanamivir ordinarily does not. Older approval ages on slide 56 need correction; see Sources.
BaloxavirUncomplicated influenza A/B, early treatment; not the lecture choice for severe hospitalized flu.Acts before viral release. Exactly 80 kg belongs to the 80-mg group; slide omits equality. Pediatric dosing has additional weight bands.
RemdesivirSelected hospitalized cases or high-risk outpatients.Useful alternative when Paxlovid interactions prevent use. Antiviral treatment is distinct from suppressing host inflammation.
Nirmatrelvir / ritonavir (Paxlovid)High-risk mild/moderate COVID-19, principally outpatient treatment.Slide 67 swaps the dose and interaction row contents. Protease inhibition belongs to nirmatrelvir; boosting belongs to ritonavir.
MolnupiravirLecture fallback outpatient option when preferred therapies are unsuitable.Mutagenesis is not protease inhibition. Lack of interactions does not make it the preferred most-effective option.
DexamethasoneSevere/critical COVID with oxygen requirement; avoid routine COVID-directed use without hypoxemia.Oxygen needed because of COVID changes the treatment logic. Transcript claim “only medication with mortality benefit” is too absolute.
BaricitinibAdd-on with systemic steroids in selected hospitalized, worsening severe/critical COVID.Not a viral polymerase inhibitor. Lecture favors it when oral therapy is feasible; no established superiority over tocilizumab.
TocilizumabSelected hospitalized severe/critical COVID with worsening oxygen needs and inflammation, with steroids.Slide CRP >75 mg/L and ferritin >1500 μg/L are lecture examples, not universal mandatory combined eligibility criteria.
RibavirinSelected severe RSV in profoundly immunocompromised patients or specialist-selected hospitalized children; supportive care is primary.Hospitalization alone does not mean every RSV patient needs ribavirin. Prevention antibodies do not treat established infection.
Nirsevimab / clesrovimabInfant prevention; nirsevimab also selected high-risk second-season children. Most infants do not need both maternal vaccine protection and antibody.Clesrovimab is first-season only. Routine second-season nirsevimab is 200 mg for eligible ages 8–19 months; slide 90-day rule is not the routine rule.
RSV vaccinesAbrysvo, Arexvy, mRESVIA in adults; only Abrysvo is the maternal product.Maternal vaccination is not infant vaccination. Prior-pregnancy vaccine does not substitute for protection of the next infant; see current guidance.

Recognition lab

Read an exposure curve

This is a schematic in arbitrary units, not measured drug data or a dosing calculator. Change the MIC and dosing pattern; explain the resulting exposure before reading the interpretation.

For a fixed curve, raising MIC lowers Cmax/MIC and AUC/MIC, and usually reduces time above MIC. AUC itself stays the same because the drug curve has not changed.

Change the infection site

PK/PD without losing the meaning

IndexMeaning / unitsLecture application
MICMinimum concentration preventing visible growth, usually mg/L or μg/mL; 1 mg/L = 1 μg/mLHigher MIC for the same drug/organism comparison → harder exposure target. MIC is not a generic ranking across unrelated drugs.
Cmax/MICPeak concentration ÷ MIC; ratio is dimensionlessAminoglycosides: preserve an effective peak; extended intervals can limit accumulation. Lecture also groups fluoroquinolones/daptomycin as concentration-dependent.
%fT>MIC100 × time unbound drug exceeds MIC ÷ dosing interval; %Beta-lactams: frequent dosing/prolonged infusion can increase time above threshold. Raising MIC at the same curve reduces this time.
AUC24/MICAUC24 = integral of concentration over 24 h (mg·h/L); divided by MIC (mg/L) yields hVancomycin: AUC24 target 400–600 mg·h/L when MIC is 1 mg/L. AUC/MIC also matters for fluoroquinolones/daptomycin; lecture grouping is simplified.
PAEPost-antibiotic effect: suppression persists after concentration falls below MICHelps explain why a high peak and drug-free interval can still work for appropriate concentration-dependent agents.

Lecture trough values: vancomycin 10–15 μg/mL mild, 15–20 μg/mL severe, historical surrogate. Do not assume either range guarantees an appropriate AUC. Toxicity rises with excessive exposure.

TMP calculation (slide 39): daily TMP mg = weight (kg) × prescribed TMP mg/kg/day. DS tablets/day = daily TMP mg ÷160 mg/tablet. Lecture example: 70 ×15 =1050 mg TMP/day; 7 DS tablets supply 1120 mg, or 16 mg/kg/day. This is a daily total, not one dose; regimen division and patient-specific adjustments require prescribing guidance.

Required drug map

Must know: target + usable site. Distinguish: the drug’s nearest alternative. Nuance: the condition attached to a rule. Trap: an attractive choice that fails one necessary criterion.

VK oral; G parenteral; benzathine G is a long-acting IM depot.Allergy; class CNS effects with excess exposure. IV G fluid/electrolyte load can affect Na/K.

Slides 11–12		Anti-staphylococcal penicillins bind PBPs.

Slides 11–12		Amoxicillin binds PBPs; clavulanate inhibits susceptible beta-lactamases and protects the antibiotic.

Gram-positive agents

Drug / source slideTarget & useExposure / regimenSafety & discriminator
Vancomycin
Slides 17–19		Binds D-Ala-D-Ala cell-wall precursors, blocking wall assembly; not a PBP inhibitor.
IV: Gram-positive organisms, including MRSA. PO: C. difficile in gut lumen. Resistance especially in E. faecium.		AUC-guided monitoring; lecture target 400–600 (AUC24 400–600 mg·h/L at MIC 1 mg/L). PO poorly absorbed; IV does not treat luminal C. difficile.Dose/exposure-related AKI; infusion histamine reaction; rare ototoxicity. Slow infusion and consider antihistamine for rate-related flushing.
Trap: Route is part of the answer. Oral vancomycin does not treat MRSA bacteremia. Infusion flushing is not automatically an IgE allergy.
Dalbavancin / oritavancin
Slides 17,20		Long-acting lipoglycopeptides inhibit cell-wall assembly; additional membrane effects vary by agent.
Gram-positive infections; approved SSTI uses. Lecture describes off-label osteomyelitis/endocarditis regimens.		IV; half-life >200 h. Oritavancin 1.2 g once; dalbavancin 1.5 g once or 1 g then 500 mg a week later for listed SSTI regimens.Infusion reactions; rare hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis.
Trap: Long half-life improves convenience but prolonged exposure matters if an adverse reaction occurs; severe-infection schedules are not interchangeable with single-dose SSTI treatment.
Daptomycin
Slides 22		Membrane binding → depolarization → disrupted DNA/RNA/protein synthesis and bacterial death.
MRSA and VRE; bloodstream and skin infection contexts.		IV, weight-based, concentration-dependent killing; no routine serum drug-level monitoring.Weekly CK for myopathy/rhabdomyolysis; eosinophilic pneumonia with fever, dyspnea and BAL eosinophilia.
Trap: Pulmonary surfactant inactivates it: do not use for pneumonia. Poor CNS penetration also limits use.

Other antibacterials

Drug / source slideTarget & useExposure / regimenSafety & discriminator
Polymyxin B / colistin
Slides 23		Disrupt Gram-negative bacterial membranes.
MDR Gram-negatives, including susceptible Pseudomonas/Acinetobacter; substantial intrinsic gaps.		Polymyxin B is active and has poor urine levels. IV colistimethate is the prodrug converted to colistin; better urinary role.Both nephrotoxic; lecture favors polymyxin B outside UTIs because of lower nephrotoxicity.
Trap: Lecture shorthand “colistin = prodrug” refers to IV colistimethate, not the active colistin molecule. Usually reserved alternatives; inhaled use is adjunctive.
Fidaxomicin
Slides 25–26		Macrocyclic antibacterial that inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase (clarification of class-wide 50S shorthand).
C. difficile treatment in the gut lumen.		Oral; minimal systemic absorption.Generally well tolerated; possible nausea; expense is a major lecture pearl.
Trap: Slide 25 says fosfomycin in this location; transcript corrects the intended drug to fidaxomicin. It is not systemic therapy.
Metronidazole
Slides 37–38		Activated intermediates damage DNA and cause strand breaks.
Anaerobes, selected protozoa; adjunct IV therapy in fulminant C. difficile, not routine replacement for oral luminal treatment.		Excellent oral bioavailability; IV:PO 1:1.Nausea, metallic taste; peripheral/optic neuropathy and rare encephalopathy; potentiates warfarin. Lecture warns about alcohol reaction.
Trap: Cefepime may need added anaerobic coverage; pip-tazo/meropenem/ertapenem already provide it.
TMP–SMX
Slides 39–40		SMX blocks PABA incorporation upstream; TMP blocks dihydrofolate reductase downstream → sequential folate blockade.
Susceptible Gram-positive/negative organisms, MRSA, Stenotrophomonas, PJP treatment/prophylaxis; UTI/SSTI. Lecture cautions against relying on it for streptococci.		IV/PO; dose calculations use TMP component. DS tablet = SMX 800 mg + TMP 160 mg. PJP treatment example: TMP 15–20 mg/kg/day.Hyperkalemia, renal injury, marrow suppression, rash/SJS/TEN; warfarin and other interactions; avoid near term/newborns because bilirubin displacement risks kernicterus.
Trap: Do not use total tablet milligrams for TMP-based dosing. Toxicities generally become more relevant at higher doses/longer courses.
Nitrofurantoin
Slides 41–42		Bacterial flavoproteins create reactive intermediates damaging multiple cellular targets.
Lower urinary infection, especially susceptible E. coli; bactericidal in urine.		PO only; rapidly removed from blood and concentrated in urine. Avoid CrCl <30 mL/min or dialysis per lecture.Pulmonary toxicity (acute or chronic), G6PD-related hemolysis, neuropathy, liver injury.
Trap: Good bladder levels do not mean good blood or renal-parenchymal levels. Fever/flank pain makes uncomplicated cystitis logic fail.
Fosfomycin (oral)
Slides 43		Inhibits MurA/pyruvyl transferase, an early cell-wall synthesis enzyme.
Main lecture role: susceptible E. coli cystitis; Enterococcus including selected VRE. Do not assume Klebsiella/Pseudomonas outcomes are reliable.		3 g PO once for standard cystitis regimen; concentrates in urine. Transcript updates slide: IV fosfomycin now exists in US, but is outside lecture focus.Usually mild GI effects/headache; cost/access.
Trap: Not fidaxomicin, not a macrolide, not the oral answer to every MDR infection.

Protein synthesis

Drug / source slideTarget & useExposure / regimenSafety & discriminator
Azithromycin / clarithromycin / erythromycin
Slides 25–26		Macrolides bind 50S and inhibit elongation/translocation.
Atypical respiratory coverage; azithromycin used in CAP regimens, traveler diarrhea and selected mycobacteria. Clarithromycin in selected H. pylori/mycobacterial regimens; erythromycin often used for GI motility.		Azithromycin: good tissue distribution, long half-life. Erythromycin: erratic acid-labile absorption.QT prolongation: erythromycin > clarithromycin > azithromycin; GI upset greatest with erythromycin. Clarithromycin/erythromycin have more CYP interactions.
Trap: Pneumococcal macrolide resistance matters. H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis are not “atypical” organisms despite the transcript grouping.
Doxycycline / tetracycline family
Slides 27–28		Primarily 30S binding → blocks aminoacyl-tRNA access and protein synthesis.

Core causal chains: forward and reverse

Why prolong a beta-lactam exposure? Normal wall assembly → A beta-lactam reaches PBPs → Cross-linking falls while drug exposure is adequate → More time above MIC improves the relevant exposure index → Frequent dosing or prolonged infusion can support killing
Reverse inference: Time above MIC → beta-lactam dosing logic (slides 8,11). Trap: The lecture dosing analogy is conceptual, not a universal renal-adjustment prescription.

Why keep an aminoglycoside peak high? Normal bacterial translation → Aminoglycoside binds 30S irreversibly → A high peak relative to MIC supports bacterial killing → A longer interval can limit accumulation → Monitor kidney function and levels when repeated doses are used
Reverse inference: High-dose extended interval is the key class concept (slides 32–35). Trap: Do not generalize this strategy to every synergy regimen or every patient.

Why does oral vancomycin treat the colon? The infection site is the gut lumen → Oral vancomycin remains mostly in the gut → High luminal exposure reaches C. difficile → Bloodstream exposure is inadequate for systemic MRSA
Reverse inference: Route determines useful location (slide 18). Trap: IV vancomycin is not a substitute for oral luminal therapy.

Why can daptomycin fail despite MRSA susceptibility? MRSA is susceptible outside the lung → Drug encounters pulmonary surfactant → Active antibacterial effect is lost locally → Pneumonia requires another agent
Reverse inference: Bug + drug + site must all fit (slide 22). Trap: Daptomycin can cause eosinophilic pneumonia yet cannot treat ordinary alveolar bacterial pneumonia.

Why do mineral supplements reduce doxycycline exposure? An oral dose enters the GI tract → Divalent/trivalent cations bind drug in the lumen → Less usable drug is absorbed → Separate dosing and preserve exposure
Reverse inference: A good drug may fail if absorption is impaired (slide 27). Trap: Doxycycline can be taken with food; the key concern is the interacting cation-containing product.

How does TMP–SMX block folate twice? Bacteria synthesize usable folate → SMX inhibits the upstream PABA step → TMP inhibits dihydrofolate reductase downstream → Sequential blockade limits nucleotide production
Reverse inference: SMX upstream; TMP downstream (slide 39). Trap: Weight-based regimens use TMP mg, not the 960-mg total DS tablet weight.

How does oseltamivir limit spread? Influenza enters via hemagglutinin-mediated attachment → The infected cell makes new viral components → Neuraminidase normally frees new virions → Oseltamivir inhibits neuraminidase → Earlier treatment limits additional infection cycles
Reverse inference: Oseltamivir → release blockade (slides 55–61). Trap: Baloxavir blocks transcription; amantadine targets uncoating and is not recommended due to resistance.

Why pair ritonavir with nirmatrelvir? SARS-CoV-2 makes polyprotein precursors → Nirmatrelvir inhibits the main protease → Ritonavir inhibits CYP3A metabolism → Viral replication is inhibited while interaction risk rises
Reverse inference: Protease inhibition and pharmacokinetic boosting are separate jobs (slide 67). Trap: Ritonavir alone has no SARS-CoV-2 antiviral activity.

Why does oxygen requirement change COVID treatment? Viral infection triggers host inflammation → Gas exchange worsens and oxygen needs rise → Dexamethasone suppresses the damaging host response → Selected worsening cases receive an additional immunomodulator
Reverse inference: Antiviral target ≠ host inflammatory target (slides 70–73). Trap: Without hypoxemia, routine COVID-directed steroids do not provide the same benefit.

How do RSV antibodies protect an infant? RSV requires F-protein-mediated fusion → An infant receives a long-acting anti-F antibody → Antibody inhibits fusion → Passive protection reduces severe disease risk
Reverse inference: Infant antibody = passive immunity; maternal vaccine = active maternal response (slides 78–79). Trap: Prevention is not treatment of established RSV.

Viral biology and timing

Influenza: enveloped, segmented negative-sense single-stranded RNA (corrected slide 51). A/B cause seasonal epidemics. HA binds; NA releases. Drift = incremental HA/NA change; shift = major new antigenic combination with pandemic potential. Incubation 1–4 days; lecture shedding roughly 1 day before symptoms and 5–10 days after onset. These are teaching ranges, not exact isolation instructions.

Antivirals often work best early because they prevent additional replication cycles. Influenza: ideally ≤48 h; severe/progressive, hospitalized or high-risk patients still warrant treatment after that. High-risk lecture groups include children <2, adults ≥65, pregnancy and ≤2 weeks postpartum. Uncomplicated oseltamivir/zanamivir courses are 5 days; peramivir/baloxavir are single-dose regimens. Prolonged severe or immunocompromised cases may require longer therapy; do not combine NAIs.

COVID: enveloped RNA virus; SARS-CoV-2 differs from other human coronaviruses. Risk of progression, early timing and drug interactions organize outpatient treatment. Oxygen requirement and inflammatory deterioration organize inpatient immunomodulation. RSV: single-stranded RNA, without influenza H/N proteins, winter predominance and reinfection; supportive care is primary. Infant distress clues in transcript: retractions/belly breathing, nasal flaring, cyanosis, apnea, poor feeding.

Vaccines: what protection means

Vaccination prepares immune recognition and can reduce severe disease; changing influenza antigens explain repeated vaccine updates and imperfect season-to-season protection. Maternal RSV vaccine generates maternal antibody that crosses the placenta. Infant nirsevimab/clesrovimab directly supplies antibody. These are complementary prevention strategies for appropriate populations, not treatments for established infection.

Influenza genome • slide 51

Slide/transcript say “double stranded RNA.” Correct: influenza has a segmented, negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome. Learn the corrected biology; ask faculty if this discrepancy becomes an assessed item.

Influenza genome ↗

Pneumonia practice item • Q4

Supplied key is azithromycin, but lobar consolidation alone does not establish atypical disease or justify macrolide monotherapy. The lecture itself warns of pneumococcal resistance. Current CAP guidance restricts macrolide monotherapy to appropriate patients where local pneumococcal resistance is <25%. The practice adaptation adds the missing context.

CAP guideline ↗

MRSA practice item • Q5

Supplied key is vancomycin. Daptomycin can also cover an MRSA skin infection. The adapted item adds D-Ala-D-Ala binding so it has one best answer. The original photo does not distinguish those treatments.

Flu ages / renal rules • slides 56–59

Slide ages are outdated. CDC treatment ages: oseltamivir FDA-approved ≥14 days (CDC/AAP also recommend younger infants); zanamivir ≥7 years; peramivir ≥6 months; baloxavir ≥5 years. Zanamivir prophylaxis is approved ≥5 years. Inhaled zanamivir usually needs no renal adjustment. Baloxavir at 80 kg uses 80 mg; avoid cation coadministration. The slide’s blanket “no interactions” and “all renal adjustments” rules are inaccurate.

Flu guidance ↗

RSV adult vaccine ages • slide 78

Lecture: >75 and high-risk 60–74, with 50–59 under study. Current CDC: all ≥75 and increased-risk adults 50–74. Preserve lecture provenance but do not memorize the older policy as current.

Adult RSV guidance ↗

RSV infant antibody dosing • slide 79

Routine first-season nirsevimab: <5 kg 50 mg; ≥5 kg 100 mg. Eligible high-risk second-season children ages 8–19 months receive 200 mg. The slide’s 90-day split is not the routine second-season regimen. Clesrovimab is 105 mg regardless of weight and not recommended for second-season use. First-season antibody is generally for eligible infants <8 months if mother unvaccinated, status unknown, or birth <14 days after maternal vaccine.

Infant RSV guidance ↗

Maternal RSV • slide 78 / transcript

Use Abrysvo at 32w0d–36w6d in the recommended season. Current guidance does not recommend repeat maternal vaccination in a subsequent pregnancy; protect the next infant with antibody as indicated. The transcript’s broad “all pregnancies” language needs this qualifier.

Maternal RSV guidance ↗

Fosfomycin vs fidaxomicin • slides 25,43

Slide 25’s “fosfomycin” in the gut-active macrolide context is corrected by the transcript to fidaxomicin. Slide 43 says only oral fosfomycin exists in the US; transcript correctly notes newer IV availability. FDA labeling confirms IV fosfomycin for adult complicated UTI, including pyelonephritis. Oral cystitis evidence must not be extrapolated to all IV indications.

IV fosfomycin FDA label ↗

Fidaxomicin target • slides 25–26

Although grouped with macrolides, fidaxomicin inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase; do not apply the ordinary 50S macrolide mechanism to it.

Fidaxomicin FDA label ↗

Vancomycin exposure • slide 18

Lecture lists troughs 10–15 μg/mL for mild and 15–20 μg/mL for severe disease as historical institutional practice. Current serious-MRSA guidance favors AUC-based monitoring: AUC24 400–600 mg·h/L assuming MIC 1 mg/L. A trough is not an exact AUC surrogate; higher exposure raises AKI risk.

Vancomycin monitoring ↗

COVID mortality and inflammatory thresholds • slides 70–73

Dexamethasone is foundational for severe/hypoxemic COVID. The transcript’s claim that it is the only drug with randomized mortality benefit is too absolute: evidence also supports selected additional immunomodulators. CRP >75 mg/L and ferritin >1500 μg/L on slide 72 are not universal mandatory paired cutoffs. Neither baricitinib nor tocilizumab is clearly superior in the cited comparison.

COVID guidance ↗

Tetracyclines and contraception • slide 27

Slide warns tetracyclines may decrease oral-contraceptive effects. CDC states most broad-spectrum antibiotics do not reduce combined hormonal contraceptive effectiveness; routine doxycycline is not an enzyme inducer. Distinguish this from interactions caused by specific enzyme-inducing drugs.

Contraception guidance ↗

PJP threshold • transcript

The spoken CD4 “250” should not be learned as the standard HIV PJP-prophylaxis threshold. NIH uses CD4 <200 for people not on/starting ART, with additional viral-load-dependent rules for those on ART. PJP prophylaxis also has non-HIV indications; the lecture’s main point is TMP–SMX’s role.

PJP guidance ↗

Terminology and overgeneralizations

MIC means minimum inhibitory concentration, not “mean”; inhibition is not identical to direct killing. AUC is total exposure, not only the area above MIC. Class kill labels are context-dependent; the transcript’s blanket TMP–SMX static label should not substitute for sequential-folate-blockade understanding. The clindamycin 2–20% slide number describes diarrhea, and toxin suppression means reduced synthesis. Macrolides inhibit elongation/translocation; tetracyclines primarily target 30S. These corrections prevent literal transcription errors from becoming flashcard rules.
